title: The Senses Quarrel With Breath
hookLine: the senses quarrel over who holds the body up, and breath settles it by getting up to leave
carry: prana holds the body; the senses follow
tomorrow: where does breath come from? a student asks too much.

lines: ONE CLAIM, CHECKED AGAINST THE PAGE.
cards: An argument breaks out inside a body. Speech says it holds the body up. So does the mind.
So do the eye and the ear. Each one is sure it's the pillar. Then breath, the quiet one, says nothing much.
It just starts to leave. And the moment it lifts, every other power is dragged up with it, whether it likes it or not.

This story sits in the second question of the Prashna Upanishad, a text built as six students asking a teacher six questions. Today: what it means by breath, and one popular claim, checked against the page.

teach.h: THE SENSES EACH CLAIM THE BODY
teach.b: Here's the scene, in paraphrase. A student asks the teacher Pippalada which powers hold a being together, and which of them is greatest. The teacher tells the quarrel.
The elements and the senses each claim the body. Breath warns them not to be fooled: it alone, dividing itself, keeps the body standing. They don't believe it.
So breath rises to go, and they all rise with it.
It settles, and they all settle, like bees following their king bee out of the hive and back again. Then the senses sing to breath, and the hymn makes it very large.

teach.h: BREATH AS FIRE, SUN AND RAIN
teach.b: Breath burns as fire, shines as the sun, falls as rain. Breath is in everything. Now the claim.
You'll hear in wellness writing that prana is basically oxygen, or that it's a hidden energy a machine can read.
The first is too small: the Prashna's breath is fire and rain and the life of creatures, not one gas in the lungs. The second is a different kind of claim altogether.
The Upanishad never offers prana as something to measure. It offers a way of seeing a living thing as held together by something it doesn't control.
Here is the teaching, named plainly: prana is life itself, the power that holds a being together, and every sense, even the mind, follows where it goes.

teach.h: A TEACHING, NOT A READING ON A DIAL
teach.b: It's a teaching about life, not a reading on a dial. What a person can actually watch is the breath itself, going out and coming back. The Prashna asks for nothing more.

how: Hindu teachers read the Prashna Upanishad's quarrel of the senses as a teaching about what keeps a being alive, and some Hindus sit with the breath as a daily practice of attention.

o: breath, prana: the life the senses rise and settle with
the oxygen your lungs take in and your blood carries
a hidden energy that a machine can measure and read

games.q: the quarrel in the body — tap the pairs.
p: each claims to hold the body up
rises to leave, and all rise too
the bees follow him out and back

s: in the Prashna, the senses rise and settle with breath, like bees with their king
breath rises to go and they all rise; it settles and they all settle.
in the Prashna, prana is just the air in the lungs
the hymn calls breath fire, sun and rain. it's far bigger than one gas.
the Upanishad offers prana as something a machine can measure
it offers a way of seeing a living thing, not a reading on a dial.

games.q: you're breath. speech, mind, eye and ear all insist they hold the body up, and they won't listen. what do you do?
o: argue louder than all of them.
start to leave, and let them feel it.
agree with them to keep the peace.
games.why: breath rises to go, and every other power is pulled up with it. they believe it then, and sing to breath.

practice: Sit comfortably and let the breath rise and settle without steering it.

As it rises, notice what rises with it, the chest, the shoulders, maybe a thought; as it settles, let speech go quiet and the eyes rest, the swarm following its king bee. If you pray, you can offer one breath back with thanks.

wordCard.voice: The breath again. In the Prashna, breath gets up to leave and every other power rises with it, like bees with their king. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: breath, life. in the Prashna Upanishad's second question, the power the senses finally praise.
